Parallelism Strategies

A model that doesn't fit on one device must be split across many.
Each cut spends traffic along its dimension to buy memory or compute.

Five collectives, then five cuts: data, weights, experts, sequence, the work itself. Each fills an earlier gap.

Prerequisite Topic 4 (the 16-byte bill) Data as of 2026-09 ⏱ about 84 min

Section 0

One device can't hold it

🎯 Warm-up: in DeepSeek-V3 training, what are a parameter's 16 bytes? — Q1 reviews Topic 4, Q2–3 preview. Safe to skip

Question 1: In standard mixed-precision AdamW, each parameter keeps five items resident in HBM. Bytes for each?

Weights (the copy for compute) bytes
Gradients bytes
Master weights (the optimizer's copy) bytes
First moment m bytes
Second moment v bytes

2 + 2 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 16 bytes. The first two are half precision (bf16), for the matmuls; the last three full precision (fp32), for the optimizer. Times V3's 671B params: 9.76 TiB (~10,000 GB), before activations.

16 bytes is the standard count, with bf16 gradients. In practice frameworks often keep the gradient accumulation buffer in fp32 (Megatron's default; V3 too): 18 bytes.

Preview (think first; answers in §2.2):

  1. Question 2: Which of the 16 bytes is biggest? Which to cut first?
  2. Question 3: DeepSeek-V3 doesn't store 16 bytes: two parts drop to half precision. Which two? Why not the master weights?

Topic 4's bill: 671B params × 16 bytes (weights 2 + gradients 2 + optimizer state 12) = 9.76 TiB (~10,000 GB) of resident training state. Top devices hold 200–300 GB, so storage alone takes 30–60 devices before any compute. So cut. But along which dimension?

Tensors can be cut along batch, sequence, hidden, layer or expert. The whole lecture is one idea:

In one sentence Traffic buys memory or compute.
A strategy picks which communication, how often, on which link.

The lecture is a relay: cut, pay one communication; find the gap, cut again.

Two rulers per cut: how often it talks (→ which link) and FLOPs per byte moved (→ stall or not; Section 3).

Glossary (from Topics 1 and 3, one line each): tensor, activations, attention head, MoE, KV cache, prefill and decode, Q/K/V, MLA, HBM, ICI, “N-way”…

Token and batch: a token is the smallest unit of text, about a word piece; a batch is a step's input, often counted in tokens here.
Tensor and hidden dimension: tensors are a model's multidimensional arrays; a token's vector is hidden-dimension long (7,168 in V3).
Activations: each forward layer's intermediate results, kept for backward.
Attention head: attention runs as dozens of small, independent attentions in parallel, each a head.
Micro-batch: one step's batch cut into a few pieces processed one at a time.
V3: DeepSeek-V3, the 671B-parameter MoE model, our running example.
Q, K, V: every token computes three vectors: Q is “what I'm looking for,” K is “what I am,” V is “what I carry.” A new token compares its Q with every earlier token's K and sums their V, weighted by similarity.
Query heads and KV heads: each head has its own Q; K and V may have fewer, several query heads sharing one KV group (at the extreme, one KV head). Inference caches K and V, so the KV-head count decides whether the cache splits by head.
Softmax: attention scores every earlier token; softmax normalizes those scores into weights that sum to 1.
MLA: DeepSeek's attention; K and V shrink to one small latent all heads share: far smaller KV cache, but only “one head” to split.
Node: one machine, usually 4 to 8 GPUs joined by a high-speed interconnect (NVLink on NVIDIA).
HBM: on-device fast memory; the model and intermediates must sit here.
Compute and bandwidth: operations vs. bytes moved, per second. Moving much and computing little is bandwidth-bound; the reverse, compute-bound.
ICI and slices: ICI is TPU chips' dedicated fast link; chips joined by ICI form a slice; slices talk via the regular data-center network (DCN).
Devices and axes: software sees one v7 chip as 2 devices, and parallelism degree counts devices; a slice's chips form a 3D grid whose x, y, z directions are the axes.
Rank: one process in the parallel job, usually one GPU (on TPU, one device).
v7 and v7x: two names for the same TPU generation (Ironwood); both appear here.
N-way: “8-way TP” means TP over groups of 8 devices. TP4 × DP2 means 4-device TP groups, 2 of them doing data parallelism: 4 × 2 = 8 devices.
MoE and experts: many parallel feed-forward blocks (experts); a small router picks a few per token, the rest idle. The parameter count is large, but each token touches only a small fraction.
KV cache: in generation, each processed token leaves a K and V that later tokens attend to; it is kept throughout, growing with context.
Prefill and decode: inference's two phases. Prefill reads the full prompt at once for token one; decode emits one per step. Decode steps are light, so requests batch up: read weights once, use them across the batch; bigger pays more.

Section 1

Five collectives

Each later cut adds a communication; meet them now. Five see daily use: all-reduce, all-gather, reduce-scatter, all-to-all, plus point-to-point send/receive. Each answers: who sends to whom, and is arriving data concatenated, summed or kept as is?

1.1 Reading the figures

A collective: devices sending and receiving under one shared rule. Figure conventions:

  • Four devices (0 blue, 1 orange, 2 green, 3 purple), four blocks each.
  • Animations: black background, a column per device (static figures: a row).

1.2 One to everyone: four basic moves

Device 0 is the root, the hub of all traffic.

See them move: four animations, one pause per step

All four funnel through the root's link; more devices, more jam. Training runs on the next group.

A closer look: how the root jams, how libraries ease it

Naively (the root serving each in turn), broadcast and reduce pile all traffic on the root, worse with every device. Libraries chain them as a relay, so the root moves one copy. Gather and scatter can't: the root holds n distinct pieces; the total stays flat, but it all crosses its one link.

1.3 Everyone to everyone: training's workhorses

“All” = everyone gets it: all-gather = gather for all, all-reduce = reduce for all, reduce-scatter = reduce, a block each; all-to-all: no sum, no concat.

1.4 All-reduce splits in two

Other work fits in between; later free wins start here: ZeRO (Section 2), tensor + sequence parallelism (Section 3).

A closer look: same AG and RS; order and what's between decide the result
  • All-reduce: reduce-scatter (RS), then all-gather (AG), nothing between; two laps of one ring (§1.5).
  • AG then RS, compute between: gather in, compute, scatter out. FSDP's weight gather (§2.3), SP's sequence gather (§3.3) and expert parallelism's all-gather token dispatch (Megatron's allgather dispatcher) fit it. We call it AGRS.
  • RS then AG, optimizer between: ZeRO scatters gradients, each device updates its share, then gathers the new weights (§2.2). All-reduce's order, plus a middle update. We call it RSAG.
  • AG and RS are transposes: a forward AG means a backward RS at the same spot, and vice versa. So SP's backward swaps their positions, yet still runs AG first: it meets the forward's exit first.
  • FSDP differs: forward has only an AG. In backward, RS is its transpose; the AG just re-gathers dropped weights.

⚠️ AGRS / RSAG are our shorthand for the order, not standard terms.

1.5 No root: the ring

With a root, device 0 receives and sends n−1 copies each: a bottleneck. Instead, link devices head to tail in a ring, no root.

The ring = reduce-scatter + all-gather. Another build shows why it wins:

The price: steps grow with devices. For small messages, per-step waits dominate, the ring loses; libraries pick by size.

A closer look: ring vs. tree, NVSwitch in-switch sums, the TPU torus

Large messages are bandwidth-bound, where the ring is near optimal; small ones by per-step waits, where many steps hurt. So libraries like NCCL pick ring, tree, etc. by message size. The NVLink switch (NVSwitch) can also sum in-switch, nearly halving each device's sends.

TPUs are more direct: ICI itself is a torus. In big enough slices (every dimension a multiple of 4) each is a closed ring; in smaller ones it's a line, the ring doubles back, and bandwidth roughly halves.

The torus adds more: each chip sits on three rings, X, Y, Z. Gathering X, then Y, then Z keeps one direction busy per step, the last heaviest. Start three data chunks on different axes (XYZ / YZX / ZXY) and all three stay saturated: the same all-gather is up to 3× faster counting bandwidth alone. Reduce-scatter runs in reverse (big step first); all-reduce's halves likewise. ⚠️ Our derivation: per-step latency ignored; XLA's chunking/scheduling unchecked.

1.6 All-to-all: a different piece for everyone

Expert parallelism (Section 4) uses the general case: unequal counts, same-route combine. Ulysses (Section 5) uses the equal-size case: a transpose.

1.7 One table to sum up

Of eight, the four rooted are building blocks; five see daily use (send/receive: Section 3's layer cut).

“Sends” = per device, ring; S = one whole copy (AllGather: assembled; ReduceScatter: before summing); Broadcast / Reduce assume a chained relay.
CollectiveDoesSendsUsed by
AllReduceSum; all get it2(n−1)/n · SData-parallel grad sync; TP: 2× fwd, 2× bwd per layer
ReduceScatterSum; one block each(n−1)/n · SFSDP bwd grads; TP + sequence parallel
AllGatherConcat; all get it(n−1)/n · SFSDP fwd weights; TP + sequence parallel; Q in KV-split inference

Two takeaways ① All-reduce = reduce-scatter + all-gather; several later cuts get free wins from it.
② Only all-to-all sends everyone different data; expert parallelism needs it, networks fear it most.
Each later cut's extra traffic is a row here. Next: the first cut, data.
Check yourself: 4 devices, one all-reduce. Ring: copies sent per device? Naive rooted: device 0?

Ring: reduce-scatter, 3 steps of 1/4 copy; all-gather, 3 more: 1.5 copies. Rooted: device 0 sends 3. More devices, wider gap.

Section 2

First cut: data

The simplest cut: each device trains on different samples. At first it doesn't fix “it doesn't fit”; only FSDP does, at a price.

2.1 Data parallelism (DP): full model per device

Every device: full model, own samples. After backward, one all-reduce averages gradients; all update. One exchange per step: rare but big (pure DP at V3's size: ~2.7 TB per device per step). Each still stores 16 bytes per parameter: still too big.

Analogy: V3's weights are a library of 61 reading rooms, one per layer, across V3's 128 branches (one per device). DP gives every branch a full copy; below, we strip duplicates.

2.2 ZeRO: shave the idlest first

Three pieces: weights (the model), gradients (each parameter's move this step), optimizer state (largest: master weights plus two moments per parameter). Ψ = parameter count.

Per ZeRO's paper, optimizer state is what stays resident across steps, checkpointed. Gradients, recomputed and zeroed each step, count separately (own ZeRO stage). Megatron sets accumulator precision (--main-grads-dtype) with master weights and moments (“precision-aware optimizer”), so some count it there.

Warm-up Q2: optimizer state is 12 of 16 bytes, so it goes first. It is also the idlest:

ZeRO-1 shards optimizer state, ZeRO-2 adds gradients, ZeRO-3 weights; each device keeps only its 1/n. ZeRO-1 also saves compute: each updates its 1/n, not all parameters.

Why are the first two stages free? The §1.4 identity:

Warm-up Q3: V3's moments are half precision; master weights (and accumulated gradients) stay full Optimizer state holds no gradients (per-step input, zeroed after use); the full-precision one is the micro-batch accumulator.
Per our accounting (2.2): optimizer state 12 → 8 bytes (master 4 + moments 2 + 2), plus 4 for the accumulator. Add compute weights (unstated; assume the usual BF16, 2 bytes): ~14 bytes per parameter (our derivation).
Master weights grow in steps too tiny to survive compression. Moments: depends on β₂ (bf16 ruler below; V3: 0.95, PyTorch default: 0.999).
A closer look: a bf16 ruler—moments compress, master weights don't

2.3 ZeRO-3 = FSDP: the last 2 bytes cost 50%

After two stages, 2 bytes of weights per parameter remain: 1.29 TiB per device for V3 at 128-way (~1,415 GB; a device has 200–300 GB). Too big. More devices can't push ZeRO-2 lower: what's left is full weights. Cutting data alone, large models need ZeRO-3, PyTorch's FSDP (Fully Sharded Data Parallel): all-gather each layer before use, discard after.

Back to the library. FSDP cuts blind to content: a room's books laid page by page in a strip, cut into 128 equal lengths, one per branch. Cuts often land mid-book: one book's tail, the next's start. Alone, a piece is unreadable. To use a room, a branch copies the other 127 (all-gather), reads, discards the copies. After backward, each piece's edits merge at its owner (reduce-scatter).

EP (Section 4) deals whole shelves, each a self-sufficient expert; FSDP's fragments serve even communication, useless until reassembled.

Communication: 3Ψ, 1.5× DP. In return, per-device resident memory drops 9.76 TiB → 78.11 GiB (~84 GB, before activations): already over V3's 80 GB H800. The data cut alone isn't enough; hence the next cuts.

⚠️ Which stages are free, which costs ZeRO-1 and ZeRO-2 are free (with micro-batches, only ZeRO-1; see “One ZeRO step” sources). ZeRO-3 costs 50% more; large models must pay.

2.4 Reach depends on frequency

DP talks once a step: slow links work. FSDP talks every layer: fast lane only.

A closer look: how far DP, FSDP, HSDP and DiLoCo each reach
  • Data parallelism, ZeRO-1: once per step, so slow links work, even across data centers.
  • FSDP: gathers weights every layer, hundreds to thousands a step (counted in §7); needs a high-bandwidth domain.
  • HSDP (hybrid sharded data parallel): FSDP in-node, DP across. Frequent gathers stay in; only gradient sync crosses (÷ in-node shards).
  • DiLoCo goes further: replicas sync only every few hundred steps, built for cross-data-center training.
⚠️ Written wrong, HSDP gradient sync can become one all-device all-reduce HSDP sums over two axes, then splits along the FSDP axis back to owners.
Cheap: reduce-scatter on the intra-node FSDP axis (1/F each), then all-reduce that 1/F on the inter-node data axis.
Expensive: merge both axes into one group, all-reduce the full gradients, keep your slice. The all-gather half rebuilds data only to discard it; the cross-node leg moves full gradients, not 1/F.
Auto-sharding (e.g. JAX's GSPMD) can emit the expensive form; we've hit it. Check: in the compiled HLO, do the all-reduce's replica groups span both axes?
Pure FSDP has one axis: no issue. Data-center boundaries don't matter; the extra data axis does.

2.5 What this cut leaves open

FSDP moves weights each step, an amount set by parameter count, not batch; compute scales with each device's tokens.

The global batch can't grow forever (too large hurts learning): more devices, fewer tokens each. Small batches cut compute, not traffic; weight movement dominates. How else to cut, adding devices without each computing less?

Versus the next cut: FSDP splits the model in form, but at heart is DP—weights are whole at compute time, each device on its own batch. The next cut keeps them split while computing.

Check yourself: which two ZeRO stages are free? Why optimizer state first?

ZeRO-1 and ZeRO-2 are free (all-reduce = RS + AG anyway; the local update between sends nothing). Optimizer state: largest and idlest, used only to update.

Section 3

Second cut: weights

FSDP rebuilds each layer's weights before computing; a big per-device batch hides that traffic, a small one can't. The second cut splits the weights instead: devices share tokens, so adding devices doesn't thin them out. Three walls: small batch stalls FSDP → TP; TP can't leave one machine → PP; PP leaves devices idle.

3.1 Where FSDP runs out: FLOPs per byte moved

Once data arrives, how often is it used? Often: the transfer hides. Once: the device waits. As a ratio, FLOPs per byte moved over the network must beat the hardware's FLOP/s ÷ bytes/s, or the device idles.

FSDP's math is clean (⚠️ our derivation, dense model): ~6Ψ bytes per step (bf16 weights gathered in forward and backward, gradients scattered once, ~2Ψ each) for 6ΨT FLOPs (Topic 4: ~6 FLOPs per parameter per token; T = tokens per device). The ratio is exactly T, whatever the model size. Intuition: each arriving 2-byte parameter is used once per local token: one multiply-add, 2 FLOPs.

Analogy: a door workshop. Craftsmen are devices; the runner, the network, carries tools (planers, jigs = weights) and door panels (activations, one per token, passed between stages). FSDP ships tools: each tool works every panel at the bench, more panels, better trips.

Red dashed line ≈ 3,845: below that many tokens per device per step, FSDP stalls. A v7 chip is 2 devices: ~7,700 per chip.

Mind the denominator: your measured bandwidth, not the spec sheet. Threshold = FLOP/s ÷ weight bytes actually gathered per second. Run a real all-gather (nccl-tests on GPUs): its busbw = size ÷ time × (n−1)/n excludes each device's own shard, so it equals actual receive bytes/s per device. At an assumed 70% of nominal, it rises 3,845 → ~5,493 (thin dashed line); an FSDP axis with few links, shared with other axes, goes higher.

A closer look: where 3,845 comes from; when it's higher

Red dashed line: 3,845 = v7's 2,307 TFLOP/s (bf16) per chip ÷ ~0.6 TB/s received per chip (the usual 1.2 TB/s counts send + receive, equal on a ring; ⚠️ this split is our estimate, see sources). The limit is the network: arriving weights are also read from HBM, but at 7.38 TB/s (12×+ the network) that line is ~313 (gray dashed, bottom), not binding. This is the optimistic line; one axis: ~3× higher. MoE on FSDP alone (no EP) moves all parameters, computes only the chosen ones: another ~18× (V3's 671B ÷ 37B).

A closer look: how “hiding behind compute” works
  • One collective, two instructions. start hands off, compute continues; done: “I need the result; wait if not here.” XLA HLO: all-gather-start / all-gather-done; PyTorch: async_op=True returns a handle, then work.wait().
  • done waits only for you: no global barrier, only your own data. Yet on a ring a slow device's data arrives late, delaying you indirectly.
  • Hiding = start earlier, done later, compute between. Prefetch: FSDP starts layer i+1's AG during layer i; backward RS is done a few layers later.
  • The cost is memory. The receive buffer is allocated at start and held until used after done; the earlier you start, the more layers are in flight. So prefetching must be throttled: PyTorch FSDP's limit_all_gathers caps AGs in flight.
  • Issued early ≠ transferred early. Channels are few; collectives on one channel queue up, so an early one behind an unfinished big one just waits. Schedule by channel queue, not just issue time.
  • Loops get in the way. JAX often writes each layer (or layer group) as a loop body (scan). start/done must pair in one iteration, so moves stay within a layer. To prefetch the next layer's weights, the compiler must move it into the previous iteration: XLA's collective pipeliner pass. ⚠️ Measured: it ignores memory when moving; overdoing it can exhaust HBM.
  • PyTorch FSDP: no loop; the runtime prefetches by layer (forward_prefetch / backward_prefetch).
  • Likewise, TP is hard to hide (§3.4): it sends activations this layer just computed, so it can't start early.

3.2 TP: cut inside the matrix

TP (tensor parallelism) cuts weight matrices; a device holds and computes a piece. NVIDIA Megatron-LM:

Two confusions. First, every device has a share of both: device 0 has half of UP and of DOWN, not one matrix each (that's splitting by layer, PP). Nothing moves between them; DOWN's partial sums are added once, moving activations. Attention too: split by head, add at the exit. So per layer: two all-reduces forward, two backward.

Second, “horizontal”/“vertical” is just drawing. We draw W1 as input × output (X·W1), so an output-dim cut looks vertical; PyTorch's nn.Linear stores output × input, so it looks horizontal. Remember: first cut on output, second on input. Megatron, drawing X·A, calls them ColumnParallelLinear and RowParallelLinear.

The order can't flip: a nonlinear GeLU sits in between:

3.3 SP: TP's partner

SP splits TP's leftover small ops by sequence: same traffic, less activation memory. Not a fourth cut, despite the name (§8.8).

A closer look: what SP splits; why traffic stays equal

TP can't split the small per-token ops (normalization, dropout, residual add), so there every device holds full activations. Megatron's sequence parallelism (SP) splits these by sequence, and each all-reduce in two: all-gather to rejoin before the TP block, reduce-scatter to split after. By §1's identity, traffic is unchanged.

3.4 TP's ceiling ignores batch

With TP, the runner carries panels (activations): craftsmen share panels, each doing part, then combine. Double the panels, and handoffs and work both double: batch cancels. Panel size is hidden size: bigger panels, more work per handoff. Tools can come early (next layer's during this one); fresh panels by default wait for the stage to end: TP traffic is hard to hide. What's left: FLOPs per byte ≈ 4.5 × hidden ÷ TP degree (⚠️ our derivation, dense layers). V3 (hidden 7,168) at 8-way TP: ~4,032. The drawn red line is most optimistic, so 8-way seems to touch it (7,168 × 4.5 ÷ 3,845 ≈ 8.4); the real line is higher, with 8-way below it (see below).

Small batch leans on TP, large batch on FSDP: left, blue is below red, so use orange; right, it has crossed, so FSDP. This assumes TP's line clears red; when both sit on or below it, as for V3, TP doesn't pay (§3.7).

A closer look: why 8-way TP is really below; two more degree limits
  • ① 3,845 assumes all three axes fully used, each a closed ring. 8-way TP spans only 4 chips (one v7 chip is 2 devices), so two discounts stack: the slice is too small for a ring (§1.5) and uses only one or two axes (§3.1). Real bar: several times higher.
  • ② Megatron by default waits for TP traffic before computing: it can't hide.
  • Attention heads split whole: Megatron needs query heads divisible by TP degree (fewer KV heads: one of KV heads/TP divides the other; bigger TP copies KV).
  • TP syncs every layer: it must stay in the fastest interconnect tier (GPUs: usually one NVLink domain).

3.5 FSDP + TP: a 2D split

Large models often use both: they cut different dimensions. Grid the devices: rows are TP groups, columns FSDP groups. TP slices weights into output-dim strips; FSDP splits each on the input dim.

Per layer: all-gather in the column to rebuild your strip (1/TP of the matrix), compute alone, add partial sums once in the row. Backward reduce-scatters gradients along columns to owners.

The math shifts: a row shares tokens but each device gathers only a 1/TP strip, so the FSDP threshold counts a whole row's tokens: ~961 per device at 4-way TP (⚠️ our derivation; measured per-axis bandwidth not applied). Hence “small batch leans on TP”: TP lends a row's tokens to FSDP. The price: TP syncs every layer, needing the fastest links.

3.6 PP: split by layer

Many machines, slow links, no per-layer weight traffic like FSDP: split by layer. TP cuts wide, PP deep:

Stages pass activations only at boundaries, point-to-point: the least traffic of any cut, so PP can cross slow links. Naively: “4 devices' memory, 1 device's speed”, one stage working at a time. So feed in micro-batches, production-line style. Planing, drilling, painting: one station each; panels flow in stacks. At first later stations wait; at the end earlier ones idle. That idle time is the bubble:

Bubble ÷ ideal compute = (p−1) ÷ m (p stages, m micro-batches). More help, but too-small ones underfeed the device.

A closer look: why activations pile up; three common fixes

Every row idles the same total: p−1 forwards + p−1 backwards. Original GPipe keeps each micro-batch's activations until its backward; at fixed micro-batch size, more of them store more. 1F1B caps those in flight at p: same bubble, less memory. Oddly, PP splits weights, yet per-device activations barely shrink: each stage holds several micro-batches.

VPP gives each device non-adjacent layer chunks: bubble ÷ chunks per device. Zero Bubble splits backward into input/weight gradients; the latter can wait to fill gaps. DeepSeek-V3's DualPipe feeds both ends of the pipeline, mainly to hide EP traffic under paired forward–backward compute (tech report sec. 3.2.1).

Going deeper: micro-batch source and size; 1F1B scheduling; uneven stage memory; DualPipe's cost

Micro-batches weren't invented for pipelines. They began as gradient accumulation: a replica that can't fit its batch share at once runs it piece by piece in time, accumulating gradients, then updates once. Pipelines borrowed this to keep stages busy. Three levels: global batch = micro-batch size × count × DP replicas. With PP, “per-device batch” is just bookkeeping: the stages form one replica on the same data. In MaxText, global batch = per_device_batch_size × device count; micro-batch = global batch ÷ num_pipeline_microbatches (must be a multiple of the stage count; defaults to it).

GPipe's extra memory: a precondition. At fixed total batch, finer splits don't change its activations (more, smaller micro-batches). The problem is a fixed micro-batch size: more of them mean a bigger batch, more activations. 1F1B's depend only on stages × micro-batch size.

How 1F1B is scheduled. Stage k (from 0) runs p−1−k warm-up forwards, then alternates one backward, one new forward (one out, one in), then drains the remaining backwards. So the first stage holds at most p micro-batches, the last 1. Why not have stage 0 send more while waiting? Steady state finishes one micro-batch per forward + backward, and a stage-0 round trip takes about p such periods. In flight = rate × time ≈ p. Extras just queue: more memory, no speed.

Uneven memory across stages. First stage holds p, last 1. Fixes: unequal layers in first/last stages (the last also has output layer, loss); recompute only early stages; park activations in host memory; or a V-shaped placement (each device owns an early and a late stage) to flatten activation peaks (Qi et al., Pipeline Parallelism with Controllable Memory, arXiv 2405.15362, Zero Bubble's sequel).

How big a micro-batch. Not “one that fills HBM”: under 1F1B, stage 0 holds p at once. Pick the smallest that fills one stage's compute. An LLM sequence is thousands of tokens, matrices are big; one or two often do; measure the knee. p = 4, 64 sequences per replica: 16 each → 4 micro-batches, bubble 3/4 of ideal time; 1 each → 64, just 3/64. Rule: micro-batches ≥ 4× stages; else VPP, fewer stages, or Zero Bubble-style ones.

What DualPipe costs. Tech report Table 2: each device stores two parameter copies (stage i forward, stage i from the end in reverse); peak activations p+1 micro-batches (1F1B: p). Aim: hide EP's ~1:1 cross-node traffic, trim the bubble. V3 can: wide EP leaves few weights per device. Chimera (2021) proposed bidirectional pipelines; DualPipe needs only even stage and micro-batch counts.

PP is for scale over slow links. Where the fast interconnect is big enough, skip it: a TPU slice puts 1,000+ chips on high-speed ICI—room for FSDP and TP—with DP between slices. So MaxText's ici_pipeline_parallelism and dcn_pipeline_parallelism default to 1; typical configs skip PP and its headaches. GPUs need PP because TP can't leave NVLink; slow cross-node links go to PP.

3.7 What this cut leaves open

Our running example, DeepSeek-V3, uses no TP; per its report, memory optimizations made costly TP unnecessary. Nearly all parameters sit in narrow expert matrices; splitting them shrinks pieces, not activation traffic. Cut along experts instead: the third cut.

Check yourself: few tokens per device—FSDP or TP: which stalls on traffic first? Why is TP stuck in one machine?

FSDP: FLOPs per byte moved = tokens per device; few tokens, transfer can't hide. TP syncs every layer; panels pass only after the stage ends, so it can't hide and must stay on the fastest links.

Section 4

Third cut: experts

MoE parameters sit almost all in the experts; the third cut puts different experts on different devices. It adds one kind of traffic, all-to-all, but brings the worst problem of any cut.

4.1 Why split the experts

Apart from its first 3 layers, V3's other 58 are MoE: 256 routed experts (8 picked per token) plus 1 shared expert all tokens use.

256 routed experts × 58 layers ≈ 653.9B parameters, ~97% of the total. TP targets one wide matrix; V3's bulk is many narrow ones, best handed out whole to devices: move the patients (tokens), don't split the doctors (experts). V3's real config: PP16 + EP64, no TP (last line).

Section 2's library: EP deals a room's 256 expert shelves to 64 branches, 4 whole shelves each; PP cuts the 61 rooms into 16 ordered stages. Whole units, usable on arrival, not FSDP's shred-and-rebuild.

4.2 EP: tokens fly to the experts

Expert parallelism (EP) communicates only in MoE layers, twice per layer, via §1.6's all-to-all, the pattern networks dread most: dispatch sends each token to its expert's device; combine sends results home.

V3 tames both: at most 4 machines per token, one copy each, fanned out on arrival; dispatch in FP8, combine in BF16.

Cost tracks machines visited: one copy each, which NVLink forwards to its experts. The report puts NVLink at ~3.2× cross-machine speed, so each machine feeds 3.2 experts on average for free: 4 × 3.2 ≈ 13, and equal traffic allows up to 13 experts (V3 picks 8).

That's training and prefill. Latency-bound decode skips in-machine forwarding: one copy per expert, so copies grow with experts picked.

4.3 EP's worst problem: data-driven load

EP's imbalance is worst: unlike other cuts, who is busy shows only after routing, and changes every batch. All wait for the busiest expert. It snowballs: popular experts get more tokens, learn more, draw more; others wither. Big-model memory buys a small-model result: a quality problem, not just speed. A two-part cure:

  • Training: make routing itself even. The old auxiliary loss on imbalance hurt quality, like forcing triage to change diagnoses; V3's ticket dispenser orders the queue instead. Each expert's score gets a bias before the top-8 pick; after each step, batch load shifts it (overloaded −0.001, underloaded +0.001). It changes who is picked, not the computed weights. A 0.0001 auxiliary loss stays as a backstop against extreme in-sequence imbalance. So V3 dropped no tokens in training; with no capacity cap, imbalance means waiting.
  • Inference: replicate hot experts across devices: EPLB (Expert Parallelism Load Balancer) and redundant experts.

4.4 Attention and experts split separately

Attention and experts differ entirely in shape (outside MoE, the EP dimension is just DP): attention's load scales with sequence and KV cache, the experts' with sheer parameter count. So the same devices can split them differently.

How much does it matter? Two names, then one measurement (box below).

The two most common inference setups: TEP (TP attention, EP experts) and DEP (DP attention, EP experts), suffixed by device count. Experts match; attention differs: one shared request batch, or one per device?

TEP spreads each request over devices: fast generation. But attention splits by head; V3's KV has one head, so every device holds it in full (§5.4). DEP keeps only each device's own requests' KV: more requests fit, experts get bigger batches. The price: all-to-all for experts, uneven load from varied request lengths, idle devices running empty forward passes. The “same devices, two mappings” figure's left setup (attention TP4 × DP2) sits between. Not Megatron's ETP/EDP (§8.6).

One measurement: a new split doubles per-device throughput DeepSeek-V4-Pro, GB300, vLLM: moving decode from TP4 to DEP8 (DP8 attention, EP8 experts) gave 2.09× a tuned TP4's per-device throughput at equal concurrency. The main gain is attention's KV, no longer copied to each of 4 devices (§5.4). Per-device attention weights are a few percent of an MoE model. Figures show V3 (32 experts/device); the test used V4-Pro.
Full accounting (devices, concurrency, time to first token) in §7.3.

4.5 What this cut leaves open

The first three cuts split batch, weights and experts, never the sequence. But activations (training) and KV cache (inference) grow with context. What if one sample outgrows one device?

Check yourself: EP's worst problem? How does V3 treat it, and why doesn't that hurt learning?

Load imbalance: all wait for the busiest expert. V3 biases expert scores, down if overloaded, up if under; it alters only routing, not the computed weights.

Section 5

Fourth cut: sequence

One sample outgrows a device? Split its sequence: the fourth cut. Training and inference split different things.

5.1 Why one sample won't fit

  • Training: per-layer activations grow at least linearly with length, plus a quadratic term without FlashAttention (Megatron sequence-parallelism paper, Eq. 1).
  • Inference: the KV cache grows per token. V3's MLA stores a compressed KV (512 dims) plus a small positional part (64): (512 + 64) × 61 layers × 2 bytes (BF16) = 70,272 bytes. × 131,072 tokens: one 128K request ≈ 8.58 GiB (≈9.2 GB), a ninth of an 80 GB GPU, for just one request. KV is the “notes” each token leaves for later ones.

5.2 Training: CP cuts activations by sequence

Context parallelism (CP) cuts a long sequence into chunks, one chunk's activations per device. Only attention is hard: every token must see all earlier ones, held elsewhere. Two fixes:

  • Ring Attention: Q is a new token's “question” to earlier tokens' KV notes. Q stays; KV circles the ring a chunk per step as each device computes the pair it holds. §1.5's ring again: the next chunk travels while this one computes, hiding communication.
  • Ulysses: attention has dozens of independent “heads.” All-to-alls before and after attention (transposes, for equal splits) flip between sequence and head splits. Split by head, each device has every token but few heads, so attention finishes locally. Per-device traffic stays flat as sequence and devices grow together. The price: parallelism caps at the head count (a whole head per device), or at the KV head count under GQA (fewer KV heads than query heads).

Why no note-passing in Ulysses? In a “chunk × head” table, later chunks see earlier ones down a column; heads in a row never interact. Ring splits rows, so dependencies cross devices; Ulysses transposes, giving each device whole columns.

Ring: people stay, notes rotate. Ulysses: re-cut so each holds a few heads of every note.

Stacked, they make USP: block the table over a 2D device grid, Ulysses' all-to-all inside a machine, a ring across; device count is the product. Megatron's CP supports this hierarchy too.

5.3 Causality unbalances the load

Generative attention is causal: tokens see only the past. Later chunks work harder, so a contiguous split swamps the last device. Fix: one light, one heavy block per device (zigzag, below).

5.4 Inference: TP copies the KV cache

In long-context, high-concurrency decode, KV often uses the most memory. TP splits by head, DCP by token. TP deals heads to devices: V3's 128 query heads split easily, but MLA's KV is one compressed copy shared by all heads: one unsplittable head.

Many models (Llama 2 70B) have 8 KV heads: 8-way TP gives each device one. Once TP exceeds the KV head count H, each head is duplicated TP ÷ H times (vLLM docs: “duplicated for tp_size / H times”). MLA's single KV head under 8-way TP: 8 identical full copies, one per device. Hence V4-Pro on TP4 (§4.4) wastes 3 copies.

DCP (decode context parallelism) stores KV round-robin by token across existing devices. Token, not chunk, because notes keep growing and new ones must spread evenly too.

The new token's Q goes to every device; each computes attention on its KV share, and the partials merge. Attention is a score-weighted average, so the rule is “don't divide yet”:

Three extra collectives per layer (vLLM default: gather Q, swap softmax denominators, combine outputs) reclaim the KV that TP duplicated; DCP degree maxes at TP ÷ KV heads, exactly the duplicates. Again: communication for memory.

Batching still works: 1,000 requests = 1,000 rows, split alike; each device does its 1/TP of all 1,000 in one step. It fits: 1/TP of the KV per device means longer contexts, more requests, bigger batches. It reads less: under MLA, plain TP has every device read the whole KV (different heads, same copy); DCP reads 1/TP, so long-context attention speeds up too.

5.5 Prefill splits its sequence too

DCP is for decode; splitting a long prompt in prefill, for a sooner first token, is PCP (prefill context parallelism). One letter apart, they're consecutive steps. In a “question × notes” table, prefill's thousands of questions split by row; decode's lone question leaves no rows, so DCP further splits that row.

Section 6 puts prefill and decode on separate machines, one each (our synthesis).

5.6 What this cut leaves open

Prefill and decode now want different splits: compute-hungry prefill a split prompt, bandwidth-hungry decode spread-out KV. Shared devices fit neither well. So stop splitting tensors; give them separate machines: the fifth cut.

Check yourself: two devices each hold a partial attention result. Just average?

No. “Don't divide yet”: each device sends numerator and denominator; sum each, then divide once.

Section 6

Fifth cut: split the work, not the tensors

Cuts 1–4 split tensors (batch, weights, experts, sequence); cut 5 splits work. A request's stages differ in character: put them on different machines, each with its own sharding.

6.1 Why prefill and decode fight

Two phases per request. Prefill runs thousands of prompt tokens through matmuls at once: compute-bound. Decode emits one token a step yet reads all weights and KV from HBM: bandwidth-bound.

Your answer is streaming word by word; someone pastes a hundred-page manual, and it stops. Voice assistants suffer more: halting speech feels slow at any average. On shared devices the engine must pick one job per step; a long prefill holds several steps while every request mid-generation waits: new requests' TTFT (time to first token) and others' TPOT (time per output token) worsen.

Decode rereads the weights from HBM each step for one use by the batch. How big a batch makes that pay?

MLA helps by shrinking the KV, so a device fits more requests. MegaScale-Infer's A100 math: a batch needs at least 156 requests; each Mixtral expert gets just 39.

Chunked prefill helps: small prompt chunks ride along with decode steps. But small chunks slow prefill (each rereads all earlier KV); the workloads still share devices and one parallelism. PD disaggregation splits them: prefill machines hand the KV cache to decode machines, which only generate.

6.2 The cost: one KV transfer

Our TPU v7x 1P1D setup (Qwen3-Coder-480B, a v7x-8 each for prefill and decode) moves KV from prefill HBM to decode HBM:

A closer look: estimating each leg
LegPathEstimate
①HBM → host memory (PCIe)~10 ms
②Host memory → peer memory (data-center network, conservatively one chip's 100 Gb/s share)~83 ms
③Peer memory → HBM (PCIe), into decode's KV pool~10 ms
Total~100 ms (10 + 83 + 10)

The middle leg: the KV for an 8K prompt is 2 (one K, one V) × 62 layers × 8 KV heads × 128 (head dim) × 8,192 × 1 byte (FP8) ≈ 1.04 GB. 100 Gb/s is 12.5 GB/s, so one trip takes about 83 ms. A CPU-side proxy also routes each request to both sides.

It is Section 1's point-to-point send/receive over the slow data-center network, affordable as each request goes once. From here on, scheduling centers on those notes: KV moves with its request. Kimi's Mooncake calls its inference system “KVCache-centric.”

Short requests, light traffic? The extra transfer and machines may not pay; stay colocated with chunked prefill.

6.3 How many machines per side

Splitting adds a knob, the prefill-to-decode ratio; balance the load. DistServe's clean example:

Rule of thumb: long prompts run 2P:1D, long outputs 1P:2D.

A closer look: the paper's best case

DistServe searches the ratio jointly with each side's parallelism. Versus unsplit systems: up to 7.4× more requests at the same latency targets (vs. DeepSpeed-MII), or up to 12.6× tighter targets (vs. vLLM) (OPT models, 90% SLO attainment). The figure's “more than double” is the paper's single-device example; 7.4× is the best over all ratios and shardings.

6.4 Separate sharding per side

The real payoff: the two sides stop sharing one parallelism.

  • Prefill machines: PCP splits a long prompt over extra devices for a faster first token (§5.5).
  • Decode machines: DCP spreads KV over devices to fit more requests (§5.4); Wide-EP spreads experts wider, so more requests feed each expert a bigger batch.
  • MoE models: often TEP (TP attention) on one side, DEP (data-parallel attention) on the other; which gets which isn't fixed: it depends on model and load (§8.6).

6.5 AFD: attention and experts on separate machines

Decode splits further: attention reads each request's own KV, binding it to the request. Experts don't care whose token it is; they want big batches, since each step reads their weights once (§6.1). AFD (Attention-FFN disaggregation) separates them: M machines only run attention, N only hold experts.

Each layer ships tokens to the experts (M → N) and back (N → M). Micro-batches rotate to hide this: one in attention, one in experts, one in flight. They split the batch (requests grouped), not the sequence: each decode request emits one token per step, so 3,000 requests make three 1,000-token groups. MegaScale-Infer needs at least three (four if communication is slow), reporting up to 1.90× per-GPU throughput.

Who uses it

ByteDance's MegaScale-Infer and StepFun's Step-3 do this; vLLM got an experimental plugin in July 2026.

6.6 Multimodal: encoder, too

Same idea, one stage earlier: the vision encoder gets its own machines and ships embeddings to the LM (encoder disaggregation; with PD, often EPD). Training's version: heterogeneous multi-module parallelism, each with its own scheme.

6.7 What this cut leaves open

Five cuts, each with its own communication and uses, coexist on a real cluster: which stay in a machine, which cross machines, whose degree comes first?

Check yourself: splitting prefill and decode adds a KV transfer. Why does it save devices?

Neither side stalls the other, so both run full: in the paper, 2 prefill + 1 decode serve 10 req/s; colocated needs 7 devices. The KV transfer is a sliver of prefill.

Section 7

Onto the machine

Real configs often stack three or four parallelisms, leaving one question: which cut rides which link. Right, and the savings hold; wrong, and the network eats them.

7.1 Fast or slow links, chatty cuts

Links differ. GB300 NVL72 joins 72 GPUs in one NVLink domain at 1.8 TB/s each (bidirectional throughout); the NIC beyond gives 200 GB/s, 9× slower. TPU slices use ICI inside (large ones form a 3D torus, §1.5); the data-center network across slices is about 50× slower like for like (conversion in Sources), far wider than GPUs' 9×.

Chattiness varies too: per-step counts (our derivation, illustrative config) span 3 orders of magnitude:

Guess first: which of TP, PP, DP gets the fast link? Picture an office building:

Default placement: TP, EP, FSDP and CP talk every layer, so they fill the fastest tier first; PP (stage boundaries only) and DP (once a step) take slow links. Also ask whether communication overlaps compute. TP's can't (each block's closing all-reduce stalls the next), so TP stays on fast links, its degree capped by that tier.

EP and FSDP can hide traffic by sending early, so some cross machines: V3's EP 64 spans 8 machines (H800's intra/inter-node gap is just 3–4×, unlike TPU's); Llama 3 puts FSDP outermost. DP moves the most data, but once a step; backward runs last layer first, so late gradients ship early. Section 6's once-per-request KV can likewise take the slow data-center network (TPU v7x).

7.2 A misplacement, up close

Same 8 devices and TP4 × DP2; only the TP groups move. Schematic: a transfer is 1 cell on a fast link, 9 on a slow one.

One color per TP group (placement 2: one per row). A step = 8 TP rounds + 1 DP: placement 1, 8 × 1 + 9 = 17 cells; placement 2, 8 × 9 + 1 = 73 (its DP pair shares a machine: 1 cell).

Hence TP rarely leaves an 8-GPU server. GB300 stretches NVLink across a rack, so EP can go wide (TP, limited by head count and matmul efficiency, rarely tops 8 or 16 even there): the fast tier's size sets how deep these cuts go.

7.3 Right cut first, then tune

Wrong placement and sharding leave tuning circling under the wrong ceiling, as we found with DeepSeek-V4-Pro on GB300. 1P1D = one prefill + one decode machine; 3P = three prefill; DEP8 = each decode device's attention serves its own requests, experts over 8 devices:

Tuning everything on TP4 decode (no eager mode, more prefill machines, concurrency) lifted total throughput 45%, but on twice the GPUs: per-GPU fell, TPOT stayed near 50 ms. DEP8 quartered TPOT at the same concurrency and more than halved TTFT.

Resharding alone bought two bigger-batch wins: no KV copy on each of 4 devices (§5.4), and twice the decode GPUs (4 → 8), halving experts per GPU. The 8 GPUs span two trays, inside the rack's fast NVLink. Check the sharding before touching parameters.

The fine print: every number, assumption and gap in the record
  • Eager mode off (CUDA Graphs on): only +2.6%; more prefill machines, tuned concurrency: total 14,563 → 21,100 (+45%); TPOT stays 46.8–53 ms.
  • Switching to DEP8 at the same concurrency of 512: TPOT 46.8 ms → 11.8 ms, TTFT 55.8 s → 22.8 s. At concurrency 256 the same setup's TTFT is only 7.8 s, so most of the 512 figure is queuing.
  • The original record doesn't break down why TPOT dropped too.
  • A GB300 tray: 4 GPUs; prefill→decode KV also rides in-rack NVLink, not NICs. Concurrency: requests queued; batch: computed at once.
  • The figure's last two rows run at concurrency 512, the first at the original script's 256. At 1,536, DEP8 reaches 65,132 total (2.47× per GPU), but TTFT hits 95 s: prefill is the bottleneck again.
  • Throughput counts prompt and output tokens. Against the first original script (1,820 per GPU), DEP8 is ~1.5× per GPU.

7.4 Choosing in five steps

Picking parallelism: five gates, each a yes/no question:

  1. Gate 1: does it fit? Weights and optimizer state too big: FSDP / ZeRO (Section 2). Too many MoE experts: EP (Section 4). KV too big at inference: DCP (Section 5).
  2. Gate 2: how big is the fast tier? Keep TP and EP within it (8-GPU server: 8; GB300 rack: 72; TPU: the slice).
  3. Gate 3: long sequence? CP for long-context training, PCP for long inference prompts.
  4. Gate 4: still short, or on a very slow link? Only now PP: small, rare boundary activations cross slow links; cost: the bubble (Section 3).
  5. Gate 5: devices left? All to DP: one communication per step, the cheapest.

Two real configurations; mind the two “not used”: V3 skips TP on 8-GPU H800 servers, Hunyuan 3 skips EP on TPU. “DP 4 × FSDP 128” is a product of shard counts.

StepHunyuan 3 (295B MoE, TPU v7, 256 chips)DeepSeek-V3 (671B MoE, 2,048 H800s)
① FitsFSDP 128 (FSDP shards experts too); any narrower OOMsZeRO-1 shards optimizer state, EP 64 experts
② Fast tier256 chips, one fast slice; FSDP already spreads experts: no EP; a small EP trial lost throughput (note below) 8 GPUs/server: no TP; EP 64 spans 8 machines (slow-link exception); ≤ 4 machines per token
③ Sequence4K / 8K, no CP4K pre-training; no CP reported
④ PPFits in one slice, not usedPP 16; DualPipe hides comms under compute
⑤ DPLeftover 4× to DP: DP 4 × FSDP 128, the default (v7 chip = 2 devices; degrees count devices: 256 chips = 512). Best: FSDP 256; freed HBM lifts per-device batch 12 → 16, +3% vs. default; widening alone costs <1%: the gain is all batchThe rest: ZeRO-1 data parallelism

Same five steps, nearly disjoint results: the two machines' fast links differ in shape. Don't copy another team's config; check your own links first.

Note: Hunyuan 3's EP test (4-way, 16 chips) lost 71% in one run, but with the batch halved (a confound); another setup lost 37%. The record blames extra all-to-all hops on the torus; at 4-way that cost is small, so the cause is open. V3: PP 16 × DP 128 = 2,048; EP 64 shards experts within those 128 ranks, no extra GPUs (our derivation).

7.5 What adding devices costs

Last question: adding devices, how much per-device efficiency survives? Two measures:

  • Strong scaling: fixed total work, double devices; does time halve? Per-device work shrinks, fixed overheads loom larger, and you hit a wall (Amdahl's law: what doesn't shrink with more devices caps the speedup).
  • Weak scaling: fixed work per device; double devices and total work; does per-device speed hold? Large-model training usually starts here, growing the global batch with devices up to the convergence cap (the critical batch size, past which steps stop falling proportionally); beyond it, only strong scaling.

The metric is scaling efficiency: per-device throughput after ÷ before. We lack clean strong-scaling data; closest: the same DP 4 × FSDP 128 at per-device batch 12 → 8 fell from 580 to 453 per chip. Less work per device hurts.

Our two measurement sets; compare within a set only. Left: weak scaling, devices and global batch ×4. Right: same devices, varying FSDP width.

Left: DP is nearly free. Four 64-chip groups do one gradient all-reduce per step: under 1% of the 23.5 s step by a rough v7 ICI estimate, even discounted for shared links (our derivation). But the groups share one slice (DP on ICI); this doesn't carry over directly across slices.

Right is the warning: same chips and batch, but FSDP over all chips instead of a quarter means more gather steps on smaller pieces, so latency stops amortizing: 11% lost. Narrower FSDP (64 or 32 shards) can't fit shards beside activations. While the batch can grow, grow it with the devices; extra devices become replicas first.

7.6 What this section leaves open

Every parallelism now has a story: what it cuts, what it sends, which link it rides. Next, a panorama and tables decode TEP8, DEP16 and DP4 × FSDP128.

Check yourself: TP, PP, DP: which goes innermost? Which can cross slow links?

TP syncs every layer, unhideable. PP: once per stage boundary, can cross machines. DP: once a step, can span data centers.

Section 8

Panorama: every parallelism in use today

So many names: DP, FSDP, TP, SP, CP, PP, EP, and for inference DCP, PCP, DEP, TEP… Just four families. Of the five cuts, weights and experts are both model parallelism. Learn the families and the names fall into place.

8.1 Four families

One criterion: what does it split? A figure, then a table:

FamilySplitsEach holdsExamples
DataData parallelismThe batch (requests) Own samples; logically full modelDP, FSDP, Attention DP
SeqSequence parallelismTokens within one sample A chunk: activations (training), KV cache (inference)CP, Ulysses, DCP
ModelModel parallelismThe weights Some columns, layers or expertsTP, PP, EP
DisaggDisaggre­gationWork phases or modules One job: prefill or expertsPD disaggre­gation, AFD
  • FSDP is data parallelism, not model parallelism. Weights are stored sharded but reassembled before each layer runs, and each device still computes its own samples. It saves memory without changing who computes what.
  • Sequence parallelism gets its own family. Strictly it splits data too (within a sample), but it exists for long context and communicates nothing like DP; lumping them blurs things.

Tables follow the four families; “New” = appeared or went mainstream in 2025–26. For reference; on a first read, skip to 8.6. Many names are new; come back as needed.

DualPipeFeeds the pipeline from both ends at onceV3's heavy expert comms must fully overlap forward/backward compute Point-to-point, overlapped with EP's all-to-allTrain

Across experts (MoE)

NameSplitsSolvesExtra commsUse
EPDifferent experts on different devicesTotal expert parameters too large Dispatch, combine: two all-to-alls. Data picks destinations, so load is uneven: EP's worst problemTrain · Infer
Wide-EP NewEP spread over 32, 64 or more devices Few experts per device, so each gets a bigger decode batchLarge-scale all-to-all; needs a dedicated libraryInfer
ETPTP inside one expertExpert too big; fine-grained: usually 1All-reduce inside the expertTrain
EDPLeftover expert-side DP, derived from the othersWhere expert gradients are summedExpert-gradient all-reduceTrain
Parallel Folding NewAttention, expert layers: same devices, two splits Breaks the old “EP ≤ DP” constraint. E.g. attention at TP4 · CP2 · DP8, experts straight at EP64 Two sets of comm groupsTrain
MoE layers get their own parallel axes Megatron training writes attention as TP × CP × DP × PP and experts as ETP × EP × EDP × PP, configured separately. Inference does the same under other names (§8.6).
Here MoE tuning has the most freedom, and the most room for error.

8.5 Disaggregation

The first three split tensors; this one splits the work: unlike jobs go to separate machines, each with its own parallelism.

NameSeparatesSolvesExtra commsUse
PD disaggregationPrefill, decode on separate machines Prefill (compute) and decode (bandwidth) hurt TTFT, TPOTKV cache transfer between machinesInfer
AFD NewAttention on one machine group, experts on another Experts pool several attention groups' tokens; ratio tunable Per-layer round trip, attention → experts → attention; hidden with 3–4 micro-batchesInfer
Encoder disaggregationMultimodal vision encoder runs aloneEncoder and LM compete for resourcesEmbedding transferInfer
Heterogeneous multi-module parallelismEncoder, LM: own parallelism eachMultimodal training: parts too unlike in shapeBridging between the two meshesTrain

8.6 Shorthands: TEP and DEP

Inference MoE configurations are usually written as shorthand plus a number, like TEP8 or DEP16. The first letter says how attention is split; EP says how experts are split.

ShorthandAttention layersExpert layers
TEP<N>TP across N devicesEP over the same N devices
DEP<N>Attention DP: each device its own requestsEP over the same N devices

TensorRT-LLM's definition, verbatim: TEP<N> shards both attention (TP) and experts (EP) across N ranks. DEP<N> keeps attention data-parallel (ADP) while distributing experts across N ranks. vLLM uses the terms the same way.

With PD disaggregation each side often picks one; no fixed rule says which gets which: it depends on model and load. vLLM's Kimi K3 deployment uses TEP8 for prefill, DEP16 for decode; TensorRT-LLM's example is the reverse: DEP4 for prefill, TEP8 for decode.

⛔ TEP / DEP are not ETP / EDP Same letters, different order, different things.
TEP / DEP (inference) describe how attention is split; DEP's D is Attention DP.
ETP / EDP (Megatron training) describe the TP degree inside an expert and which devices expert gradients are summed across.
The Megatron repo has zero hits for TEP / DEP. Treat them as two vocabularies; don't translate between them.

Other combined terms you'll hear:

  • 3D / 4D / 5D parallelism: only counts kinds used at once, and projects count different dimensions. TorchTitan's paper calls FSDP + TP + CP + PP 4D; Megatron's Parallel Folding paper calls TP / EP / CP / DP / PP 5D. Citing one? Name the dimensions.
  • TensorRT-LLM's “Hybrid ETP”: TP + EP mixed in expert layers; not Megatron's ETP.

8.7 Mistaken for parallelism

The test: does it split a new dimension? If not, it isn't new parallelism.

NameWhat it actually is
TBO / SBO / DBOComm hidden in compute: two staggered batches, one talks, one computes
Async TP, TP comm overlap, collective matmulStill TP, with comm and matmul chopped small and interleaved
EPLB, redundant expertsLoad balancing: replicate and re-place hot experts. An EP fix, no new dimension
Offload, recomputationTrading time for HBM, or host memory for HBM
Chunked prefillInference scheduling: long prompts chunked, mixed with decode, less blocking (§6.1). Not §8.3's Chunked PP (prefill too): its chunks flow down the pipeline: a new axis

8.8 One name, many meanings

TermWhat it means where
SPAt least three: Megatron's SP (LayerNorm-type segments only, with TP); DeepSpeed's SP (Ulysses); any sequence splitting. Megatron: splitting all activations = CP
CPTraining: split activations. vLLM has two switches: PCP adds devices and cuts TTFT; DCP adds none and expands KV capacity
DPDense: separate replicas; MoE inference: really Attention DP, per-step sync
ETPMegatron: in-expert TP; TensorRT-LLM Hybrid ETP: expert layers mix TP + EP
hierarchicalZeRO++ hierarchical sharding ≠ Megatron hierarchical CP
GPU / chip / device1 GPU = 1 device; a TPU v7 chip = 2 to software; degrees count devices
BandwidthOne-way or send + receive: here 1.8 TB/s (NVLink) and 1.2 TB/s (ICI) are combined; 800 Gb/s and 100 Gb/s (NICs) one-way
Concurrency/batchConcurrency: requests queued; batch: computed at once

8.9 Three questions to take away

Unfamiliar parallelism name? Ask three questions ① What does it split? (data, sequence, model, or the work itself)
② What communication does it add? (one of Section 1's five)
③ Which link should it ride? (chattier per step → further inside; §7's office building)

Try the opening's V3: PP 16, EP 64, ZeRO-1 data parallelism (report sec. 3.2). PP cuts depth, sends only at stage boundaries, so it crosses machines; EP cuts experts, two all-to-alls per layer, so ≤ 4 machines per token; ZeRO-1 cuts data: one reduce-scatter + all-gather a step, cheapest. Three cuts, three collectives, three links: V3's cryptic config (PP 16, EP 64, ZeRO-1) now reads plainly.

⭐ Back to the opening: where to cut. The five cuts split different things but pay one price: spend communication to buy memory or compute. Picking a parallelism strategy is picking which communication to pay, how often, on which link.

Last, with the ruler from Sections 3 and 6: the hardware line is compute ÷ bandwidth; how you cut sets the workload line. Each cut here tries to lift a workload line above it.

Two after-lecture questions (answers are above; think first. Sections 1–7 each end with a “Check yourself” too)

① An MoE model will decode on one GB300 rack (72 GPUs, one NVLink fast domain). How would you split its attention and expert halves? Answer the three questions, then compare with 7.3.
② TEP8 vs. Megatron's ETP8: only the letter order differs. How do the meanings differ? Look it up, then see 8.6's red box.
